Larry Ridley
Bassist Larry Ridley was born in Indianapolis, Indiana on September 3, 1937.

He played with Freddie Hubbard and Wes Montgomery as a teenager and went on to perform and record with many prominent jazz artists. Larry recently retired as professor from Rutgers University and is currently the head of the IAJE African American Jazz Caucus.
Larry was interviewed in Toronto, Canada on January 10, 2003 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and we are in Toronto at the IAJE convention. I’m extremely pleased to have Larry Ridley with me today.
Thank you, Monk, my pleasure.

You have had a marvelous career in different parts of the music. And I’m wondering if when you were a boy or a young man at what point did you set your career path? Is it possible — was it that definite of a time?

Well I think that there are little pivot points that sort of set the tone for what my destiny — if I can use that word — was to be. I think my spiritual values came from the time that I was an altar boy in the African Methodist Episcopal Church. My brother and I, my brother that’s next to me, we were both at an early age, seven years old or something like that. And my mother was originally a Baptist so I came up through that whole African- American tradition of Baptist church and then the African-American Episcopal Church. So certain spiritual values, and then my family, I came from a very large family. My mother came from a family of 13 kids. So the get-togethers at my grandparents’ home was always like a mini-United Nations. And I became very early aware of the differences in personalities and people like this. So a combination of those kind of spiritual aspects and also recognizing the differences that exist among people. And as I’ve grown older you know you realize all of these things transcend ethnicity or the limitations of ethnicity, you realize that human beings are human beings. And you begin to just look and see what are those things and you do a quick study on being able to have insight into understanding that and how to not be unnerved by certain types of situations. I started playing music when I was three years old, playing the violin. In fact I had like a little tiny violin it was about that size. And unfortunately I had some pictures, and I like to think that they were cute, everybody says that they were cute, but I think a lot of them were lost in memorabilia that my parents had in our home in Indianapolis and so it’s up here. So God knows. But the music thing, and then I had an uncle, Ben Holliman, who was a © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
gentleman who befriended Hoagy Carmichael. In fact my Uncle Ben always told me that the major part of the song “Stardust” was his.
Oh my.
A lot of people are not aware of this. And Hoagy was very close to my uncle for all of his life.
And your uncle was a musician?

Yes. He was an entertainer and he was a good friend of Eubie Blake. In fact Eubie Blake told me stories about how they met. Eubie was traveling through Indianapolis, Indiana and Eubie was kind of down on his finances. So he went to the local pool hall and he was an excellent pool shark. And he kind of played down his ability and he told these guys, “Yeah well I’d like to shoot a few rounds” and they set up the limits for whatever the wager would be. And so he proceeded to just kind of take it easy and then after a while he immediately started running the table on them. And these guys were ready to jump up and guys were pulling out their knives and everything, talking about, “We’re going to cut this guy.” And my uncle knew all these guys and being that Eubie was a stranger just passing through, you know they didn’t know who this guy was and they say oh this guy comes in and is going to set us up and take all our money. And so my uncle saved him from these guys. Which I thought was a great story.
It is a great story.
And Eubie acknowledged it.
He never would have reached a hundred.

My uncle didn’t tell me that, Eubie told me that, which is great. So playing music and then as I was a kid I was a part of a music club and all the young musicians around town like Freddie Hubbard, Virgil Jones, Mel Ryan and David Hardiman, on and on, we all came up playing jazz. And the Montgomery brothers, Wes, Buddy and Monk were there. And Monk befriended me, and it’s very interesting how as a young teenager — well first, how I came to play the bass was I went to a Jazz at the Philharmonic concert. And Ray Brown, Herb Ellis and Oscar Peterson and Ella Fitzgerald did a set that just totally knocked my socks off. And I said — because I’d been playing the violin — but I said that is what I want to do.
This was in Indianapolis?
In Indianapolis, yes.
At about what year would it have been?
Oh God I can’t remember. I was about twelve or thirteen years old so I can’t do the math.
So maybe ’47?
Somewhere around in there, yeah. Somewhere around in there. And I got a bass, and there was a friend of mine at the high school who had a bass, had one of those old tin © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
basses that they had, because they confiscated most of the wood and the plywood that the King Company were using to make basses. So they made these tin basses.
I’ve seen one of those.

Black tin bass. And this guy came from a fairly well-to-do family and his parents just gave him everything. And he just had this bass. So I talked him into letting me borrow it for a while. And I taught myself how to play the bass.
Was jazz, before this seeing Ray Brown, was jazz part of your household?

Oh yes. My parents were into Duke Ellington, Count Basie. My mother’s youngest brother was into the more current stuff like with the bebop and stuff like that. And all these musicians around town, you know, like were all very supportive. There are so many names I hesitate to name a lot of names, but I mentioned the main ones like the Montgomery brothers and David Baker. David Baker was there and he is a few years older than me but he’s like my big brother and he’s always looked out for me. In fact when I went to Yale University we were roommates. And my mother always told him, said, “David now you make sure that he studies.” David and I roomed and we had bunk beds. And David used to always pull me out of the bed and I have to say that David Baker is one of the — I’m fortunate to have a brother like him. Even though we’re not blood brothers we are brothers. Because he has taken care of me since I was a young guy and he’s always been there for me and he’s always encouraged me, and he’s a phenomenal person. You know when they start talking about who’s the dean of jazz education, it’s David Baker. Because he was one of the first — he and Jerry Coker were one of the first guys, and then John Mehegen came along with his books trying to define and articulate in a codified way, improvisation. Because most of what we learned, I mean we used to transcribe guys’ solos and try to figure out how they were doing this over the chords and this, that and the other. But David was one of the first to start putting this in a form that was accessible to teach how to play jazz and Jerry too. Jerry is a very dear friend too. And then Jamie Aebersold came in as a freshman at Indiana University when I was there, and David was there, and that’s how he got his start. Because he was a protege of David Baker also.
Can you imagine that any of them could envision where that led? You know this gathering here is astounding to me.

Well that’s what’s so beautiful about it. We were dealing with it as a labor of love not particularly knowing which way it was going to go. And I was very fortunate to be involved early on, as David refers to one of the Renaissance men of trying to get jazz in. When I went to Indiana University, 1955, I saw how the European art form and classical players were moving in and out doing their gigs and coming back to the university to teach. And I said if the seed was planted then, I said someday I’m going to try to do what © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

I can do to make sure that jazz becomes recognized. Because I always recognized that in order for jazz to be truly recognized as a legitimate art form that there is going to have to be an acceptance by the Academy in quotes.
At that time, ’55, was there resistance in that Academy?

Oh most definitely. Most definitely. And it’s only really started to lighten up to a certain extent over the past few years. But I mean the old man that started Berklee College of Music, he was one of the first people that started something in the Boston area — Mr. Berk. And you see the behemoth that they’ve become. And I sometimes lament the fact that some of the direction I know that he wanted things to go had sort of been absorbed into a much broader range now so that it’s beyond Berklee’s — their modus operandi is much broader than just jazz. They are reflecting on being contemporary.
Contemporary music, yeah. Which is cool.

But jazz, recognizing its roots in Africa and coming through the African-American experiences and then incorporating all the other elements that it has done, you know I think that it’s important that that be emphasized in all jazz degree curriculums. And also it should be taught on the elementary, secondary and the higher education levels. Because Mary Lou Williams came up with this thing about the living tree of jazz. And if we are going to recognize this art form as a living tree you have to recognize the roots. And if you don’t continue to fertilize and nurture those roots in order for it to keep growing new branches and new leaves with the cyclical forces of nature, which is what life is all about, it dies. And it loses a certain fundamental part of what it’s about. And it’s important. I mean what they teach, the European style of music, I mean they go back to the Gregorian chant and bring it through. So when you study it that’s what you know. There’s a continuum. And the same way with jazz. It’s not saying that we don’t have music that’s in a certain stage. That’s one of the things I’m trying to emphasize with the hip hoppers and also the people who are doing the quote unquote smooth jazz, that they have to understand the continuum of how this music evolved. And when they talk about Africa they have to recognize that it’s not just the simplistic definition of jazz as being African rhythms with European melody and harmony. There was melody and harmony in African music. And that’s what Duke Ellington used to always talk about. Even though he reflected and he was wide open to the music of Ravel, Debussy, Satie, you name it, all the great European art music composers, it was how it was utilized and how that was synthesized into what was essentially African derived music.
Would it be safe to say that the melodic part of the African music that filtered into jazz was more of a vocal nature, the way they sang?

Well of course. I mean see the thing is that those vocal things are also a part of the instrumental techniques that were translated. Because it’s a sound in your ear. That’s why © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

a lot of jazz musicians in terms of the academic community would always say oh those jazz musicians play out of tune. Because they don’t recognize it’s coming from a different source. And it’s not going to have that kind of thing because it’s not that type of music in its purest form. So you can’t use that as a barometer to negate or whatever. It’s all music, but all musics have their particular parameters that codify what that music is. So in understanding — and there’s also the argument in the African-American community about this because a lot of them would like try to put jazz down and say oh that’s the Devil’s music as opposed to the spirituals which led to the Gospels. And it’s all a matter — those same musical techniques are utilized. When you hear Aretha Franklin sing “Amazing Grace,” and when she sings the blues she’s still using the same technique. So it’s a question of the sacred text versus the secular text. And that’s the only difference. Thomas E. Dorsey, who is considered the father of Gospel music, was a jazz piano player. He played jazz. And then he found a niche of moving over into that particular arena. And the Gospels, people tend to forget that the Gospels grew out of the spirituals. And a lot of those things came out of the old African chants and things like that. So there’s that tie. You can’t chop it off and say that it started now. No, no. We all are the sum of many parts — S-U-M — and we are also a part of a tradition and a legacy. But there are a lot of people who are not being taught that and the insight into understanding how important it is if you truly want to be a person of substance you must go back and you must — I used to tell my students all the time at Rutgers — I was there for 28 years — and I told them I said look just don’t take everything I say as being total Gospel. I want you to cross reference what I am telling you. Because that’s what I’ve done in arriving at the conclusions that I have. And it’s important for you so that you are truly ingrained with feeling that you are confident in taking the stance in the posture you have. You’re entitled to your own ideas and your feelings about a lot of things. But make sure that your points of view are responsible and well thought out and well researched. And that way you don’t find yourself caught in the cross about all these things. If somebody says, “Well how do you know that?” Well going back you can begin to tie it in. So you’re just not making wild assumptions. Case in point there’s a thing in the new Jazz Times where Gary Giddins is talking about Kenny G. And I must check with Gary to find out if this is really true but supposedly in an interview with Ted Pankin, who is with WKCR FM in New York, the Columbia University jazz radio station, they feature a lot of jazz because Phil Schaap is there. Kenny G supposedly attributes the fact that Charlie Parker got his nickname Bird because he had something happen with his reeds and it sounded like he was chirping. Now I hope — I didn’t mean to mess up my interview, it was Monk talking about Kenny G. But I mean I’m just using that as an example as a case in point of what I’m talking about, how a person in his position who has gained his own personal © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

mission and I have no problem with him, that’s what he does, it’s music that you can talk over, have in the background. It’s not like when I hear Charlie Parker and I stop and say oh wow, check that out what he did going through that chord change. You know Kenny’s found his niche and hey, God bless him. He’s doing his thing. But it’s just very interesting when people in situations like this take it upon themselves to make these wild assumptions and to misinform people. And we need to do away with that kind of stuff. And if he doesn’t know the answer to a certain kind of thing he doesn’t have to fabricate anything. And that’s what a lot of people do. It’s the problem with a lot of writers and a lot of critics. They don’t do their homework, they don’t check with musicians, they don’t understand the musician’s point of view. They don’t take the time to understand. They don’t study the history of the music because it’s still just their opinion. But many of them are in certain positions where they can make or break, just like the theater critics do with plays that are on Broadway or other things. They make or break peoples’ careers with what they say. But I think that all of these people who put themselves in that position and sort of posture themselves as being authorities or experts need to make sure that they have really, really done their homework. Otherwise I don’t want to talk to them. I really don’t. And the whole thing about jazz polls. I had a long conversation with Leonard Feather. Leonard Feather told me that the jazz polls started because as a young man coming here to the United States he was totally enamored with jazz. And he expected when he came to the states that he was going to find these jazz musicians wearing nothing but the finest clothes, riding around in limousines and having these fantastic women on their arm and living in mansions and blah, blah, blah. He had this whole fantasy going. When he gets here he finds out a lot of these musicians were just struggling and starving. So he went to the magazines and started pitching them — why aren’t you talking about these great musicians that you have here? And they told him point blank he said, we are only interested in selling magazines. If you can come up with an idea that will help us to sell magazines we’ll be glad to incorporate that. So that’s when he came up with the Esquire and Metronome and the Down Beat polls and that’s how that became a factor in the jazz community. And it’s kind of gotten out of hand because it’s become very political, I mean a lot of people don’t know but the ballot boxes are stuffed. It’s almost like the Florida election.
Oh you’re kidding.

Where we finally, or for the first time, had a president elected by the Supreme Court as opposed to the President appointing the Supreme Court. But that’s another story, right Monk? But some of the same elements. Like people stuffing the ballot box, and industry buying time and promoting their artists and this, that and the other, so it becomes incumbent upon them — the Grammys — we know that that’s all political. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Wow. Well those are great statements. And I’m curious as to whether music played a big role in your church? LR; Oh yes.
And did you get involved in that music in your church as a young boy?

Couldn’t help it. It was part of the environment and you didn’t even think of it as some sort of separate component. It was just the fabric of life. As I look back over it as we see the way things are being broken down, oh yes, Milt Jackson came up in the church and he did this and that’s the reason why he’s playing the vibes the way he plays the vibes. Well when he was coming up he wasn’t thinking about that as something separate and apart from — it’s just a part of the everyday lifestyle. You know you’re hearing it all the time. I’m hearing this music. So it was just natural. I’m around all this spiritualism, the various preachers and stuff like that, they’re a part of your community, you know them. You are participating in church activities. It’s just a way of life. And my parents, I’m very blessed that I have such great parents who gave me the opportunity and exposed me. We didn’t have a lot of money but we weren’t wanting for anything in terms of the true, spiritual food. And that’s what counts. And my mother and my grandfather always taught me — because I came up under the heavy racism and segregation and went to segregated schools, all that whole thing. And I was a part of a token group that was allowed to integrate the high school that I went to. And it was based upon what kind of I.Q. that I seemed to exhibit to them and they thought well we’ll let the colored kid in.
No kidding. So this would have been —
1951. In Indianapolis, Indiana.
In Indianapolis.
Where the Ku Klux Klan was thriving. Believe me.
Did this group of students that you were included in, what was your reception like with your fellow white students?

You know young people are a lot more flexible than older people think sometimes. And of course there were some people that were aloof and strange and may have come from homes that taught them to have somewhat slanted maybe potentially racist viewpoints. But for the most part we were just kids. We just had a ball. The guy I was telling you about that I got this bass from, this tin bass, he was a white kid. We were buddies. We didn’t think about it. His name was Mike Phillips. Mike and I were just — I mean we were just pals. We didn’t think about the fact that I’m African-American or Negro or whatever the terminology was during that particular time. Colored or anything like that. I was just a pal. We had similar things that we enjoyed and it brought us together. I mean God is good. And I don’t think things happen by accident. And you learn these kind of things and it’s about human values. Yes there are differences and we have different © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

cultural things that are different. But we can coexist. I can appreciate you. I mean I don’t look at you and say oh yeah Monk is a white guy. You are just a friend. You’re just a guy that I like and we have — there’s a chemistry between us, and the vibes between us, there’s nothing hostile about what we are feeling. I don’t have any predetermined opinions about who and what you are. I come together to dialogue with you. See people spend too much time talking at or to. They don’t dialogue with. It’s not about monologue. It’s about win-win situations. I’m not going to get a hundred percent of what I want and you’re not either. But we learn how — I mean thinking people — truly thinking spiritual people think along the lines, in my opinion, of learning how do we coexist? How do we win-win? And how do we — if I have a difference of opinion about a certain thing, let’s engage in discussion. Let me share with you why I feel the way I feel and let me hear why you feel the way you feel. And let’s leave it so that we’re both open to the fact that it’s not carved in stone in terms of what our opinions or our feelings are at that given moment. Because education is an ongoing process. And once you stop learning, you’re dead. Because studies have been conducted where they say the percentage of our brain power that we utilize, and the averages are very small when you consider it in the ratio of zero to a hundred percent. It’s over here somewhere, more towards the zero side. And then you get people who are very brilliant and they’re stretching that thing saying hey wait a minute, I want more of this. Because we’re all just passing through and we’re trying to — because I believe that this is not the final destination. I really believe that. A friend of mine — just a little quick comical anecdote, because I like to use a levity on occasion, but a friend of mine told me he says the reason why he believes in reincarnation is because he says you look at Colonel Sanders. He keeps killing those chickens and they keep coming back. I know it’s corny. I’m from Indiana, what can I say, Monk?

It’s okay. You’re right, there couldn’t be an endless supply of those chickens. When you got close to graduation in high school, what kind of career, what were your prospects? What were you thinking of?

Well I was fortunate in that Freddie Hubbard and James Spaulding and a lot of us, we had our own little bands and we were playing jazz. In fact we had a hot little band. My uncle was friendly with some gentlemen who owned a club in Indianapolis. And we had a gig, we worked six nights a week with two matinees, and we were just teenagers. We were playing all the Art Blakey Jazz Messenger, Clifford Brown, Max Roach charts and everything. And we had a piano player by the name of Al Plank, a white guy who lives in San Francisco now, been living there for several years, and he was — he was not out first pianist, we had another guy Walt Miller who was the original pianist — but then Al Plank came in. And Al had the ability to help write a lot of arrangements and then Freddie and we all contributed some stuff to the repertoire. But we gained a reputation © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
throughout the midwest in terms of our little group. And I had my first road gig when I was sixteen, with Conte Candoli.
Was this the Jazz Contemporaries?
The Jazz Contemporaries, yeah. That was the group.
With Conte Candoli?
No Conte Candoli, that was something —
I’m sorry, I missed what you said.

The group with Freddie Hubbard and Jimmy Spaulding and first Walt Miller then Al Plank and Paul Parker was the drummer. And then we used to play with Wes. The first time I saw Monk Montgomery and I approached him about taking lessons from him he told me, “Well come over to the house, kid.” I went over to the house and there is Wes sitting up there with the guitar and his brother Buddy at the piano. A saxophone player by the name of Pookie Johnson and the drummer Sonny Johnson. They called themselves the Montgomery-Johnson Quintet and they had a steady gig working in a place called the Turf Club. So Monk says, “Go over and pick up the bass.” I said, “What?” “Go over and pick up the bass.” So I went over and picked up the bass and they struck up a tune. And I’m saying wait a minute, what’s happening here. He said, “Look kid, I’m going out to the west coast because I’m beginning, starting a group called The Master Sounds, and I’m going to have to go out there to set up some business and I’m going to be gone for two weeks and I want you to fill in for me.” “Yes sir, Mister Montgomery.” And here I was man, that was his way of teaching me. He never really gave me a lesson other than me absorbing and listening and watching and listening to him perform. But as far as saying okay you do this and you do that, I taught myself that in the very beginning. And of course I knew from playing the violin you know, so I taught myself the bass clef and all that. And then I had great teachers on the violin. I had a young lady who was with the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra who was my teacher. There was a woman by the name of Ruth MacArthur who had a conservatory there. She was a young African-American woman who set up a conservatory, and Slide Hampton and his whole family and all of us used to go there. And she had a relationship with the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra where she got some of the players to teach us, in the African-American community. And they would come in and give us lessons. And so we had excellent training. And then there was some gentlemen there who were excellent mentors who taught, Mr. Russell Brown, Mr. James Compton and Laverne Newsom who taught at the high school and also in the elementary schools, Mr. Lawrence Leggett who taught me in the third grade when I was in my little elementary school orchestra. And so we had excellent instruction. And the thing was learning about it, and what I learned from Wes, it was so important, that I tried to reflect to my students how important, part of playing jazz and playing music period is © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

having good ears. You know because when you’re up there improvising you’re not thinking about oh I’m going from a D minor seventh with a flat five over here to a G seven with a raised nine. You’re not thinking about all that. You’ve got to sit at the piano and you’ve got to get that sound, or the guitar, and get those sounds in your ear and know how to respond to that improvisationally through hearing lyrical lines. And that’s one of the things I’m concerned about that is happening with jazz education. Too many of these kids are coming through and they sound like computers because they’re learning how to play licks and patterns but they’re not learning how get their own personal sound. And that’s what jazz is all about, finding your own identity. I don’t try to play the bass like Ray Brown or Paul Chambers or Richard Davis or any — Charlie Mingus. You know? I have learned how to be Larry Ridley. Because — as the Bible says, to thine own self be true. Of course I’ve learned from them and there are certain things that I have picked up from them but I don’t try to just say oh, that’s not the way Ray played it so I’ve got to go back and try that again. It’s not about that.
How can you foster that ability to invent melodies and what happened to you with this — being thrown in that situation? How can we do that now?

They’ve got to learn tunes. The more songs that you know that have melodic content — the brain is like a computer. You have to — if you put garbage in you’re going to get garbage out. So you have to put something up there. And one of the things that I always stress to my students when they’re in the workshops and things I do, how many melodies do you know? I’ve done artists-in-residencies in different places. I will never forget one time I was at the University of Utah. I asked the young people what do they want to play. They says let’s play “Giant Steps.” I said, “Excuse me?” Okay. Blues in B flat. They said, “But we said we want to play ‘Giant Steps.’” I said, “No, you have to show me that you can play the Blues in B flat, or any key for that matter, before you can talk about ‘Giant Steps,’” I said, “because I came up around John Coltrane. John Coltrane, see you all come in at these different stages of hearing people. And see Coltrane is so beautiful because his career is documented on recordings. You can hear the growth. See all that stuff that he was playing at the end, he could still go back and walk the bar, which is the basic stuff in the community.” I remember a woman coming up to Sonny Stitt, he came through Indianapolis playing at this club and he was up there just taking it easy because he thought well I’m in Indianapolis I’ll just kind of take it easy. This woman came up to him and she says, “Sonny Stitt, let me tell you something. I spent my last five dollars to come in here to hear you play because I like your music.” She said, “But you better stop bullshitting on that stage or I’m going to take one of these chairs and go upside your head.” So he said, “Oh, excuse me, madam” and commenced to bear down and start playing. And it’s that kind of thing. You know like but they have to know melodies. They © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
have to learn tunes. They’re learning too many things like exercises that take you through the two-five-one progression. Or I’m going to play the Dorian or the Lydiot or Idiot scale.
I like the Lydiot.

Or the demented scale. And they have to understand that you’re composing music. And you have to relate to your audience. Nobody wants to come and hear you practice. I don’t want to come and hear you sit up and play exercises. I mean do that in your house or in your practice room or something like that. You have to learn how to compose music. That’s the beauty of jazz. You’re called upon to be an instantaneous composer. You have to learn how to build your solos. I hear these kids, they’re just playing ad infinitum. Well let me show you everything I’ve practiced today. No. That’s not music. When you listen to Bach, Beethoven, any of those European art music masters it’s just like writing — that’s why I always compare it to English composition even. You know you have to have an introduction, you introduce your theme, your thesis, you develop it, you recapitulate, you do a summarization and then you lock up and bow as Kenny Dorham used to say. Kenny used to say, “Get two choruses of your best shit together baby, and lock up and bow out.” And Charlie Parker used to say, “It’s always best to leave people wanting more.” And Milt Jackson used to tell me, “Once you get past the third chorus you’re practicing.”
That’s so interesting because also, those guys had to operate in a time when the length on a record was very limited.
That’s right.
They couldn’t go on and on and on.

Well Max Roach was telling me that when the 78s were, that sometimes you would only get four bars. And even in playing in the bands. And that’s what spawned a lot of the jam sessions because guys were frustrated because they wanted to improvise and stretch out more. But sometimes in a band you might have one tune that was your feature for that night, and if you acted up with the band leader you might not even get to play it that night. So then you’d leave there a nervous wreck. “I didn’t get a chance to really do my thing.” You know. And the thing is when you go back and listen to those records by the Freddie Websters and Lester Youngs, they didn’t play a whole lot of choruses. And Charlie Parker used to always say that. Leave them wanting some. Roy Haynes told me when he was first playing, was basically auditioning for the gig with Lester Young, he was playing and he was just slam-banging and everything and he was going through his stuff. Papa Jo Jones. And Coleman Hawkins. When I worked with Coleman Hawkins I used to just sit up for hours with him just asking him. Miles Davis is Miles Davis. Fats Navarro. On and on and on. We can do that on all the instruments. And what makes them special is because they are themselves. And if you’re not trying to find your own identity I mean Ernest Hemingway is not trying to be William Shakespeare. Bach wasn’t — you know Mozart wasn’t trying to be Bach. Stravinsky was not trying to be Wagner. People in the arts, just like actors and actresses. And it’s true in all professions when we look at it. So it’s not something that’s just only in music or even in art. Gauguin and Rembrandt. Renoir. All these people are different. They found their thing that becomes them. Frank Lloyd Wright. I.M. Pei.

Well that’s why I think that people like myself and I have other people who are disciples like I am in recognizing how this can be a problem. And it’s true in anything. was some of the stuff that early people say oh that music was born in the brothels and houses of ill repute. Allison, yeah. Okay.

Guess what? A man with this kind of knowledge. He went around to the machines and was a chip collector. Putting it in — you know, cleaning up. Because they wouldn’t hire him because of his color. You know that kind of craziness. I mean here’s a man, who knows what he could have contributed if he had been given the opportunity. That’s why I try to tell the young African-American kids now — you don’t realize the dues that people paid. And this whole thing about getting out to vote? Hey, I came up through that thing. You know I was friendly with Rap Brown and Amiri Baraka and all these guys and Stokley Carmichael, all these guys. And people want to put the Panthers down, like Huey Newton and Bobby Seale and all them. Those guys — they started out, the government and other nefarious groups that painted the picture of them being the enemies of the state. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

They were just being very outspoken about what they knew that the community needed to do and the kind of racist barriers that were being placed on us. And they were crying out and they wanted to see something — they didn’t pick up guns just to be some kind of warring militia group. They knew that that was the only way. These weren’t no Bible toting — they wanted to talk that Bible toting stuff but you talk about a contradiction. Don’t pass that bullshit to me because I know. I was with my father when I was a kid and my brother and I and we were going through a lot, a used car lot in Indianapolis. And I was about six years old. And you know how little kids are, you get in the car and you’re trying to act like you’re driving. And I’ll never forget this guy looked — to me, as a six year old, he looked like he was about seven feet tall. A white man, he came and pulled me out of the car and said, “You little curly haired Nigger” and kicked me right in the crack of my ass. I felt every bit of that man’s shoe in my ass, and kicked me so hard I pissed on myself. And I’ll never forget that. But I’m not bitter about it. But it just taught me something. I learned a lesson from that. And my father, and the way my father handled the situation taught me a lot about maintaining my cool. Because naturally my father came to my defense. But he didn’t get into no thing where he probably would have been hauled off to jail and this, that and the other. He handled it so diplomatically. And he put the man in his place and let him know that he was totally out of order. Here’s this little kid, what was he doing? He can’t even reach the pedals. He can barely shift the gears. What are you talking about? You know these are the days of the clutch. I’m talking about 1941 Plymouths and stuff like that. This is before dyna-flow and all this other stuff with the automatic gearshifts and all that stuff. No way — what was I going to do with that car? And I wasn’t in there trashing the car or anything like that. But I’ll never forget that and it taught me something. And not just in terms of relationships between black and white people, but there’s good and bad in every ethnic group. It’s just like now I feel bad about the kind of rap that people who are Islamic are getting. That there’s all this racial profiling that’s going on. People have to be very careful about that. And I know everybody’s very uptight. Look I saw, in my apartment in New York in Manhattan I looked out my window, I was up at twenty minutes of nine to answer the telephone and I looked out my window and had a straight shot of the Twin Towers right from my bedroom. It was just like a straight shot from my bedroom window I could see that. I saw that building on fire. I thought it was just a fire. And I said well maybe the sprinklers are going to put it out but I couldn’t believe what was happening. And the next thing I know, bamm. And New York became — Manhattan became an armed camp with the National Guard the state and local police. It was one of the most traumatic things anybody would want to go to who © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

has never been in a war zone. You were literally in a war zone. I couldn’t even go past a certain point, perimeter, in my neighborhood unless I could produce I.D., a driver’s license that stated I lived in a certain area, they wouldn’t let me go. And I needed to go out of town and I couldn’t even get out of the airport because the flights were all canceled. And I needed to have a pair of pants altered, you know, some cuffs put on my pants, I couldn’t even go to the tailor because the National Guard guys wouldn’t let me go into the block. They said you have no business there, you don’t live there so you can’t go. I said but I’ve got to get my pants fixed man, I’m not a terrorist, I just need to get my pants fixed. The tension and everything that existed in that city, but the way people came together. New York is a beautiful place. Because in spite of the fact that people think New York and people ask me how can you live in New York oh my God. People getting mugged and this, that and the other. But New York has got the best of the best, it’s got the worst of the worst, and all the different — it’s yin and yang and everything in between. And to see how people came together. And people were in tears and it was just a very traumatic experience. I didn’t know what had happened to my youngest brother. He worked for the Social Security department right down in that area. And I was worried about him all day and finally in the afternoon I went out to the post office and I was coming out of the post office which is right across the street from where I live. And I see this guy standing up there and he’s got all this ash and stuff on him, it was my brother.
Oh my Lord.

And he saw me and he was just — like he was in a daze. And when he saw me he just grabbed me. He’s taller than I am and he was just beating me, “Oh Larry, oh man, I’m so glad, do you know man I could have been in that building, it could have been me, we were talking to one of our colleagues who was in the building and we were telling him to get out and the guy was talking about they’ve told us to stay, that just sit tight, he said, and he’s gone now.” You know so I had to take him, I took him up to my apartment. He had walked all the way from the World Trade Center up to where I live at 14th Street and Avenue A. And I took him upstairs and we went and got a six pack of beer, because I had to settle him down. And he took a shower and I gave him a sweat outfit of mine to put on so he’d have some clean clothes. But you see all these kind of things, it’s all related to the music. People might watch this and say well we got off on a tangent.
That’s all right.

But it’s a part of what we’re talking about in terms of the human condition, the human existence. And all that’s a part of the music. And when a person gets up to improvise they have to reflect that in their music and that’s a part of who and what you are. And so this whole thing about the jazz education and how commercialized it is in certain instances, © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
we just have to be a watchdog to make sure that people understand that we cannot have this sort of cookie cutter instantaneous way of producing things.

really. And everybody is rushing to get — now they’re able to make their own CDs. And I was talking with some of the people from WBGO-FM in Newark.
